content: The care of sick neonates and infants, including the identification and referral of seriously ill infants, can be effectively extended to those suffering from severe acute malnutrition. The group emphasized the importance of existing recommendations, even if they are not specifically tailored for infants with severe acute malnutrition. These include the WHO guidelines for feeding non-breastfed children aged 6–24 months (2005) and the WHO integrated course on infant and young child feeding (2006). This underscores the value of maintaining and reviewing growth-monitoring charts at the primary healthcare level for infants and young children. Severe acute malnutrition in infants under six months of age can be classified as either uncomplicated or complicated. Uncomplicated cases can be managed in outpatient settings, while complicated cases require inpatient care. The potential benefits of inpatient treatment must be weighed against risks such as nosocomial infections. The guideline development group acknowledged that generic infant formula milk can be safely provided in some inpatient settings. However, mothers or caregivers who are expected to continue formula feeding after discharge must receive clear guidance on the safe preparation and use of replacement feeds. This information is included in the WHO integrated course on infant and young child feeding. The group also stressed that when formula milk is provided as part of the management of severe acute malnutrition, it should be implemented appropriately to avoid undermining public health messages about exclusive breastfeeding for infants under six months of age. This issue was discussed during a 2004 WHO meeting, where participants concluded that infants with edema should be fed F-75 during the stabilization phase. However, F-75 was deemed inappropriate for severely wasted infants without edema, for whom generic infant formula or diluted F-100 would be safer. It was noted that no data were presented at the meeting to substantiate these conclusions. There was consensus that undiluted F-100 should not be given to infants under six months of age due to its high renal solute load and the risk of hypernatremic dehydration. In some settings, ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) is being given to infants aged 5–6 months as a pragmatic response when exclusive breastfeeding is not feasible. However, there is no evaluated evidence to confirm the safety or effectiveness of this approach. The group identified an urgent need for research in this area. The recommendations align with existing WHO guidelines, such as the Management of Severe Malnutrition: A Manual for Physicians and Other Senior Health Workers (1999) and the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) guidelines (2000). Severe acute malnutrition in infants aged 0–5 months is defined as a weight-for-length less than -3 Z-score or the presence of bilateral pitting edema. Infants with poor weight gain who do not respond to nutritional counseling should be admitted for further investigation and treatment. Any infant with a general danger sign, as defined by IMCI, should also be admitted for urgent care. Infants under six months of age with severe acute malnutrition and complicating factors, such as recent weight loss, ineffective feeding, or pitting edema, should be admitted for inpatient care. They should receive the same general medical care as older infants with severe acute malnutrition, including parenteral antibiotics for possible sepsis and treatment for other medical complications. Feeding approaches should prioritize establishing or re-establishing effective exclusive breastfeeding. If breastfeeding is not possible, appropriate replacement feeds, such as generic infant formula or diluted F-100, should be provided with guidance on safe preparation and use. Infants admitted to inpatient care can be transferred to outpatient care when all clinical conditions and complications, including edema, are resolved, and the infant demonstrates good appetite, clinical wellness, and adequate weight gain. Discharge from all care is appropriate when the infant is feeding effectively, has adequate weight gain, and achieves a weight-for-length of ≥ -2 Z-score. The guideline development process followed WHO evidence-informed procedures, including systematic reviews and consultations with experts and stakeholders. The recommendations were based on the best available evidence, even though the quality of evidence was often very low. The group emphasized that these practices are standard care principles that benefit infants with severe acute malnutrition without significant risk of harm. The guideline also highlights the need for further research on topics such as the predictive value of growth indicators, effective therapeutic feeding approaches, and the re-establishment of breastfeeding in malnourished infants. The WHO aims to support countries in adapting and implementing these guidelines to improve the management of severe malnutrition globally.
